section_summary: This section contains four patent disputes involving American firms and Japan: rejected iron-reduction patent applications, Japanese patents on American printing equipment, allegedly infringing toy boats, and imported watch straps. Correspondence and internal memoranda show the State Department weighing informal representations while repeatedly directing firms toward the applicable patent laws and legal procedures.

people.name: J. Prindle

subfiles.title: General Reduction Corporation case jacket
subfiles.about: Identifies the General Reduction Corporation patent-rights case in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jacket for correspondence concerning protection of the corporation’s Japanese patent rights.

subfiles.title: Prindle, Bean and Mann request for intervention
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The firm requests a protest over Japan’s rejection of two iron-reduction patent applications.
subfiles.summary: The attorneys describe William H. Smith’s inventions, patents granted elsewhere, and the Japanese rejections. They allege discriminatory policy and ask for prompt United States representations before a May deadline.

subfiles.title: Department reply on rejected patent applications
subfiles.about: The Department requests fuller legal and factual support before considering informal discussions with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks whether General Reduction Corporation exhausted Japanese remedies and seeks the rulings and reasons for rejection. Foreign patent grants alone do not establish its rights in Japan.

subfiles.title: Additional copy of April 6 patent protest
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: A partial additional copy repeats the firm’s complaint about rejected iron-reduction patents.
subfiles.summary: Partial copy of the April 6 letter, ending mid-argument on Japanese treatment of patent applications.

subfiles.title: General Printing Ink Corporation case jacket
subfiles.about: Opens the case containing the General Printing Ink Corporation patent dispute.
subfiles.summary: Jacket marking the start of a separate patent case.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs routing note
subfiles.about: A handwritten note requests a draft reply and mentions an earlier pump-infringement matter in Korea.
subfiles.summary: Requests a reply; notes that S. Miller, formerly at Seoul, can discuss the matter.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on challenging Japanese patents
subfiles.about: The memorandum considers how General Printing Ink Corporation could seek invalidation of Japanese patents.
subfiles.summary: Advises the company to give its evidence to a patent lawyer in Japan.

subfiles.title: General Printing Ink Corporation complaint
subfiles.from: General Printing Ink Corporation, Export Division
subfiles.about: The company alleges that Japanese customers patented printing machinery it had supplied and now obstruct its sales.
subfiles.summary: The company describes its metal-decorating press and drying oven, Japanese customers’ later patents, and lost business. It asks whether United States officials can secure cancellation or assignment of those patents.

subfiles.title: Department reply on Japanese printing-machinery patents
subfiles.from: J. F. Baker, Acting Solicitor, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that the company must challenge the disputed patents through Japanese legal procedures.
subfiles.summary: The Department declines to obtain cancellation or assignment itself. It outlines Japan’s five-year period for contesting patents, encloses relevant law and treaty material, and offers names of private counsel in Japan.

subfiles.title: Pridwin Industries case jacket
subfiles.about: Identifies the Pridwin Industries patent-protection case in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jacket for the correspondence on allegedly infringing Japanese toy boats.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch on Pridwin toy-boat complaint
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The consul forwards Pridwin’s complaint, his proposed reply, and invoice information on Japanese toy-boat exports.
subfiles.summary: The consulate had difficulty identifying manufacturers and buyers. Garrels encloses correspondence and Yokohama invoice data, and asks the Department to consider releasing information normally withheld.

subfiles.title: Pridwin Industries inquiry about Pop-Pop boats
subfiles.about: Pridwin seeks information about Japanese makers and representatives of toy boats it says infringe its patents.
subfiles.summary: Pridwin asks the consul to identify Alps Toy Company and other makers of candle-heated steam toy boats sold in the United States.

subfiles.title: Invoices covering Pop-Pop boats
subfiles.about: The list records certified invoices for Japanese toy-boat shipments to American purchasers.
subfiles.summary: Lists six February–March 1934 shipments, with shippers, suppliers, purchasers, quantities, and prices.

subfiles.title: Consulate reply to Pridwin Industries
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The consul reports findings on the makers, exporters, and American buyers of the disputed toy boats.
subfiles.summary: The consulate identifies numerous small manufacturers, links Alps Toy Company with Kuramochi, and confidentially lists exporters and American purchasers. It says the Japanese design patent had expired.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser memorandum on releasing consular letter
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends forwarding the consular reply to Pridwin despite usual Department practice.
subfiles.summary: Recommends an exception to normal practice because of widespread alleged theft of industrial property in Japan.

subfiles.title: A. Sauer and Company case jacket
subfiles.about: Identifies the case concerning alleged Japanese infringement of A. Sauer and Company patents.
subfiles.summary: Jacket for the tubular watch-strap patent correspondence.

subfiles.title: Economic Adviser routing memorandum
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends that the Legal Adviser’s office draft the response to Sauer.
subfiles.summary: Explains the delayed handling and refers the patent questions to the Legal Adviser’s office.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Legal Adviser note on Sauer patents
subfiles.about: The note considers treaty protection and whether Sauer had secured patent rights outside the United States.
subfiles.summary: Suggests Sauer may hold only United States patents; much of the handwritten OCR is unclear.

subfiles.title: Senator Donahey’s referral
subfiles.about: The senator forwards Sauer’s request and asks for a direct reply to the company.
subfiles.summary: Transmits an attached communication and requests a direct answer to its writer.

subfiles.title: A. Sauer and Company complaint about Japanese watch straps
subfiles.about: Sauer asks how to protect its United States watch-strap patents against low-priced Japanese copies.
subfiles.summary: The company cites its patents, an American infringement suit, and Japanese straps offered far below its price. It asks for assistance against the competition.

subfiles.title: Department reply on Sauer’s patent protection
subfiles.about: The Department explains patent rights in Japan and offers possible informal diplomatic inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Assuming Sauer holds only United States patents, the Department finds no present basis to oppose manufacture in Japan. It quotes the industrial property convention’s priority rules, explains that infringement claims follow local law, and offers to ask Japanese authorities about informal action if Sauer supplies details.

subfiles.title: Ramsey and Rave clarification of Sauer’s request
subfiles.from: Joseph A. Rave, Ramsey and Rave
subfiles.about: Sauer’s attorneys clarify that they seek to stop imports into the United States, rather than manufacture in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The attorneys cite Albert H. Sauer Jr.’s United States patents and the harm from low-priced imported copies. They acknowledge that a domestic injunction is possible but ask whether imports can be stopped before the straps are distributed.

subfiles.title: Department reply on stopping watch-strap imports
subfiles.from: Green H. Hackworth, Legal Adviser, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department addresses whether allegedly infringing Japanese straps can be barred from entering the United States.
subfiles.summary: The Department knows of no procedure beyond an injunction for excluding the straps on the stated facts. It suggests consulting the Secretary of the Treasury about possible administrative assistance.
